impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model of expected function calls are directed to an abstract idea under step one of the Alice framework for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment, holding that the asserted claims of the '322 and '115 patents are abstract at step one of Alice, reversing the district court's denial of Norton's § 101 defense. The court also held that the district court erred in denying JMOL on damages for foreign sales, and remanded for further proceedings on Alice step two. This decision impacts cybersecurity patent holders and software patent portfolios broadly.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies accused of infringing broadly-claimed software patents gain a stronger basis to challenge patent eligibility, particularly for claims framed as comparing observed behavior against models—a common pattern in cybersecurity and AI patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in software and cybersecurity fields face increased risk that their claims will be invalidated as abstract ideas under Alice step one, and the ruling restricting damages from foreign sales limits recoverable damages in global technology disputes.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims directed to methods of treating headache with humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for lack of written description and enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering methods of using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies. The court found the specification's disclosure of antibody G1, combined with known methods of making humanized antibodies, was sufficient. This decision preserves Teva's patent protection for its Ajovy product against Lilly's competing CGRP-targeting drug and has major implications for biologics patent scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies benefit from a more permissive standard for written description and enablement of genus claims covering biologics, supporting broader patent protection for antibody-based therapies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents in the biologics space, potentially delaying market entry for competing CGRP-pathway treatments and other antibody therapies.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the jury's finding that asserted information constituted protectable trade secrets under California law was supported by legally sufficient evidence, and whether ideas that are generally known in an industry can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation and breach-of-contract claims, holding that plaintiffs failed to prove their asserted information qualified as protectable trade secrets because the concepts were generally known. The court also reversed the patent inventorship correction, finding that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting verdict and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against trade secret claims benefit from the court's rigorous requirement that plaintiffs must demonstrate each asserted trade secret is not generally known, raising the evidentiary bar for trade secret plaintiffs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face heightened risk that their claims will fail if the underlying concepts overlap with generally known industry practices, even where specific implementations were allegedly misappropriated.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the three-year statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit, given evidence that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years prior to filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and JMOL denial in favor of Insulet on its DTSA claim against EOFlow for misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets, holding that Insulet's claim was time-barred as a matter of law. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing suit. This is a significant ruling on DTSA statute of limitations analysis.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a powerful defense where the plaintiff had constructive or actual knowledge of the alleged misappropriation well before filing suit, enforcing the strict three-year DTSA limitations period.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering or having reason to discover misappropriation, as delay beyond the three-year DTSA limitations period will bar claims regardless of the strength of the underlying evidence.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner that granted an exclusive license but retained the right to sue for infringement and other exclusionary rights retains sufficient constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that the patent owners retained sufficient exclusionary rights—including the right to sue for infringement and control over sublicensing and assignment—to satisfy Article III standing requirements despite granting an exclusive license. This clarifies standing doctrine for patent owners who license substantial rights but retain enforcement powers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners who structure licensing agreements to retain litigation rights and approval authority over sublicenses and assignments can maintain standing to enforce their patents, providing flexibility in monetization strategies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face a narrower path to dismissal on standing grounds when patent owners have carefully drafted license agreements to preserve exclusionary rights.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and rejection of VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether the court properly struck certain damages theories for failure to disclose them in damages contentions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement of the '836 patent related to multicore processor task allocation, finding genuine disputes of material fact on extraterritoriality, and remanded for further proceedings. The court affirmed the striking of certain damages theories for inadequate disclosure. This ruling has implications for semiconductor patent enforcement involving products with global design and manufacturing processes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting infringement of semiconductor and processor patents benefit from a broader view of domestic infringement activity even where design and manufacturing occur partly abroad.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued exposure to infringement claims for products designed or partially manufactured abroad but used or sold domestically, and must ensure rigorous compliance with damages disclosure requirements.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate deposition witness may testify beyond personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether computer source code constitutes hearsay under the Federal Rules of Evidence in the context of an on-sale bar defense under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the pre-AIA on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters outside personal knowledge at summary judgment and that computer source code commands are not hearsay statements. This ruling strengthens the evidentiary tools available to defendants asserting prior-art defenses based on historical product sales.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity gain broader ability to use corporate representative testimony and source code evidence to prove prior art sales, even when original engineers are unavailable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges based on historical corporate testimony from witnesses who lack direct personal knowledge of prior art products.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents relating to non-uniform constellation designs for digital communications, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court affirmed findings of infringement and damages. This case provides important guidance on the eligibility boundary for claims involving mathematical optimization applied to specific technological implementations in communications standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies implementing communications standards benefit from the partial vacatur of eligibility, potentially narrowing the scope of enforceable patent claims covering mathematical concepts applied to signal processing.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims covering signal processing innovations must ensure their claims are directed to specific technological implementations rather than abstract mathematical optimization to survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in pharmaceutical composition patents refers to pH measured at a standard temperature in the field, and whether Actelion was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement and no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents for Actelion's epoprostenol patents. The court upheld the construction that pH values in the claims must be measured at the standard temperature convention in the field. This decision impacts pharmaceutical patent enforcement for formulation patents where measurement conditions affect claim scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from a claim construction approach that ties technical terms like pH to standard measurement conditions, limiting the scope of formulation patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies face narrower claim scope for formulation patents when measurement-dependent claim terms are construed according to field-standard conditions rather than conditions that would expand infringement coverage.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it previously filed a declaratory judgment action and missed the deadline for seeking a stay of that earlier action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that BioMarin could not obtain a mandatory stay of Ascendis's refiled declaratory judgment action under § 1659(a)(2) when BioMarin had missed the deadline to seek a stay of the original action. This prevents parties from using tactical refiling to reset statutory deadlines for mandatory stays, preserving the ability of declaratory judgment plaintiffs to proceed in district court alongside parallel ITC proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies seeking declaratory judgments of non-infringement can proceed in district court without facing mandatory stays when the ITC respondent missed its original deadline, preventing gamesmanship through tactical refiling.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC complainants who miss the § 1659(a) deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action cannot cure the deficiency by encouraging the opposing party to refile, limiting strategic options for controlling parallel proceedings.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report for unreliable methodology and then granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated the summary judgment in favor of Microsoft, holding that the district court applied an overly restrictive standard in excluding the expert's opinions on reasonable royalty damages for patents related to virtual network optimization. The case is remanded for further proceedings, emphasizing that damages experts should be given reasonable latitude in methodology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a more permissive appellate standard for admissibility of damages expert testimony, reducing the risk that otherwise viable infringement cases are dismissed at summary judgment due to excluded damages evidence.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending patent suits face greater difficulty in excluding damages expert reports at the Daubert stage, potentially increasing the likelihood that cases proceed to trial.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watch models that infringed Masimo's patents covering wearable blood oxygen measurement devices, including the Commission's domestic industry and validity determinations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 through importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen features that infringed Masimo's patents. The court upheld the limited exclusion order, the domestic industry determination, and validity findings. This high-profile ruling sustains a significant import ban on one of Apple's flagship products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with established domestic industries gain confidence in the ITC as an effective enforcement venue, particularly for wearable technology and medical device patents against major importers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies importing products with patented health-monitoring features face sustained exclusion orders that may force product redesigns or licensing negotiations to maintain market access.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination of sensor-based logistics patent claims, particularly regarding claims requiring reporting sensor information after a predetermined time delay.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that all challenged claims of FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further proceedings. The court also addressed concerns about Qualcomm's standing to petition for IPR given it was not a party to the underlying infringement litigation but filed petitions on the same day as the co-defendant's deadline. This decision has implications for third-party IPR petitions and IoT/logistics patent validity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners in the IoT and logistics technology space benefit from a more rigorous obviousness analysis at the PTAB, and may gain protection against third-party IPR petitions filed by entities not involved in the underlying litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on IPR challenges filed by third parties to invalidate competitor patents face uncertainty about the viability of such strategic petitions.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representative organizations were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that PACER fees exceeded statutory authority. The court upheld the settlement's fairness, the attorneys' fee awards, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, rejecting an objector's challenges. This decision provides important guidance on settlement approval in government-fee class actions and the permissibility of incentive awards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Class action plaintiffs and their counsel benefit from affirmation that large settlements with the federal government over excess fees can be approved, and that incentive awards to organizational class representatives remain permissible.

impacts.caseName: Fortress Iron, LP v. Digger Specialties, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder may use 35 U.S.C. § 256(b) to judicially correct inventorship to add an unreachable co-inventor, and whether patents are invalid for omission of a co-inventor who cannot be located.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's holding that the patents were invalid due to omission of a co-inventor (Huang) who could not be located, and denied Fortress's request to judicially correct inventorship under § 256(b). The ruling emphasizes that patent holders bear the burden of ensuring correct inventorship and that inability to locate a co-inventor does not excuse the omission.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain a strong invalidity defense when patent applicants fail to name all co-inventors, particularly in cases involving foreign collaborators or contractors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that collaborate with foreign manufacturers or contractors on inventions face significant risk of patent invalidation if co-inventors cannot later be located to correct inventorship, even where the omission was not deceptive.
